specAnchors.text: Core practical 3: investigate how insulating materials can be charged by friction (physics only)

primer.text: This core practical hangs a rubbed polythene rod from a cradle and brings other rubbed rods close — never touching — to watch attraction and repulsion do the talking. Rod material is the variable under test; rubbing time, cloth and rod length are controlled. The analysis sorts polythene and acetate onto opposite charge signs.

modules.title: Apparatus, variables & method
modules.opening: The set-up is deliberately delicate: a polythene rod hangs from a cradle on nylon string so the smallest electrostatic nudge can swing it. Each test rod is rubbed with its own cloth and brought close without contact — any touch would drain the charge and end the experiment.
keyPoints: The experiment tests how friction charges rods of different insulating materials.
The rod material is the independent variable; the charge gained is the dependent one.
Rubbing time, cloth type and rod length are the controlled variables.
A polythene rod hangs from a cradle on nylon string so it can swing freely.
Test rods are brought near, never touched, or the charge would leak away.

low.restatement: Rub a rod with a cloth, hang another rod on a string, and watch whether they push apart or pull together.
low.analogy: Two magnets on strings: hold one still, bring the other near, and the swing tells you the sign.
low.examPointer: Name the variables precisely — independent (rod material), dependent (charge), controls (time, cloth, length).

medium.restatement: The cradle isolates the hanging rod from hand contact, and the no-touch rule protects the transferred charge from leaking to earth through fingers.
medium.analogy: A held-back detective at a crime scene: observing from a distance keeps the evidence intact.
medium.examPointer: Apparatus questions expect the full suspension kit: cradle, nylon string, wooden stand.

modules.title: Analysis: polythene vs acetate & evaluating
modules.opening: The result table writes itself: a rubbed polythene rod gains electrons from its cloth and charges negatively, while an rubbed acetate rod loses them and charges positively. The hanging rod's response sorts every test rod — rotating away means like charge, swinging in means opposite. Careful evaluation then covers draughts, misread swings and a numerical upgrade.
keyPoints: Rubbing transfers electrons from one insulator onto the other.
A rubbed polythene rod gains electrons and charges negatively.
A rubbed acetate rod loses electrons and charges positively.
Repulsion by the hanging rod means like charges; attraction means opposite ones.
Small deflections can be misread; more rubbing transfers more charge and a clearer swing.
A numerical variant counts paper circles picked up, giving graphable data.

low.restatement: Polythene goes negative, acetate goes positive; same-sign rods push apart, opposite-sign rods pull together.
low.analogy: Two people wearing matching football shirts push away from each other's fans; rivals mix freely.
low.examPointer: Answer in electron language: gained electrons = negative, lost electrons = positive.

medium.restatement: The observed swing is a force comparison, so its direction is trustworthy but its size is qualitative — which is why the paper-circle variant adds numbers.
medium.analogy: Reading a compass versus a protractor: direction is reliable, magnitude needs an instrument.
medium.examPointer: Evaluation marks sit in two places: shielding from draughts/vibrations, and the numerical dependent variable.

glossary.definition: The quantity the experimenter changes — here, the rod material.
The quantity measured — here, the charge gained by the rod.
The suspension loop that lets the hanging rod swing freely.
The loss of stored charge through contact with another object.
